entries.label: adjective phrase
entries.meaning: Extremely cheap; costing almost nothing.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk about prices, rent, food and travel. It works after *be* (*It was dirt cheap*), after verbs like *buy* or *get* (*I got it dirt cheap*), and before a noun, usually with a hyphen (*dirt-cheap flights*). It normally means a great deal, but it can also hint at low quality.
entries.pattern: be / get something dirt cheap; a dirt-cheap + noun
examples: Gas was **dirt cheap** when my dad was in high school, like thirty cents a gallon.
We found a **dirt-cheap** flight to Denver, but it leaves at five in the morning.
I got this couch **dirt cheap** from a neighbor who was moving across the country.

drill.sentence: Rent in that little town is {{dirt cheap}}; you could get a whole house for what we pay for a studio.
drill.hint: costing almost nothing (two words, the first a noun; not *so* or *super* + adjective, not *a steal*)

entries.related: *a steal* — a great bargain; *cheap as chips* — the British equivalent; *dirt poor* — extremely poor.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something you get for free, usually a small item a business gives away to promote itself, or a small service done without charge.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech: *They were handing out freebies at the fair.* It also covers a favor someone does without charging you (*This one's a freebie*). Hotels and formal ads say *complimentary* instead (*complimentary breakfast*).
examples: The bank was giving out **freebies** at the street fair: pens, tote bags and little bottles of sunscreen.
The mechanic didn't charge me for checking my tire pressure; he said, "This one's **a freebie**."
My sister signs up for every store's birthday club just for the **freebies**.

drill.sentence: The kids came home from the parade with a bag full of {{freebies}}: candy, stickers and little flags.
drill.hint: things handed out at no cost (not *giveaways*, *goodies* or *samples*)

entries.related: *a giveaway* — something given free, often in a promotion or contest; *swag* — free branded items from companies and events; *on the house* — offered free by a bar or restaurant.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To spend a lot of money quickly and carelessly on something, often something you don't really need.
entries.usage: Casual and a little critical, or self-mocking when you say it about yourself: *I blew my whole bonus on a new TV.* The object is money, an amount or a paycheck, often replaced by *it* (*blow it all on*); the past forms are *blew, blown*. *Splurge on* is more positive: a deliberate treat.
entries.pattern: blow + money / an amount / your paycheck + on something
examples: I **blew** my entire first paycheck **on** a new phone and then couldn't make rent.
Don't **blow all your money on** souvenirs the first day of the trip.
My uncle won five hundred dollars in the lottery and **blew it** on a weekend in Vegas.

drill.sentence: Our aunt gave each of us fifty dollars and made us promise not to {{blow it}} all on candy.
drill.hint: spend it carelessly (two words; not *waste it* or *spend it*)

entries.related: *splurge on* — spend a lot on a treat, on purpose; *waste money on* — neutral and critical; *blow through* — use up money fast (*blow through your savings*).

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To divide the bill at a restaurant or bar so that each person pays part of it.
entries.usage: *Check* is the usual American word for a restaurant bill; *split the bill* is also common in the US and is the normal British form. *Split it evenly* or *split it four ways* means equal shares, while *separate checks* means each person pays for their own order. It's fine at a work lunch too.
examples: There were six of us at dinner, so we **split the check** and each paid about forty bucks.
Excuse me, could we **split the check** between these two cards?
On our first date, I offered to **split the check**, but she insisted on paying.

drill.sentence: Everyone ordered about the same thing, so let's just {{split the check}} four ways.
drill.hint: divide the restaurant bill (three words, American; not ending in *bill*)

entries.related: *go Dutch* — each person pays for themselves, a bit old-fashioned; *pick up the check* — pay for everyone; *separate checks* — each person gets their own bill.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Wait patiently for a while and don't act yet, usually until someone gets back to you or something is ready.
entries.usage: Common in American speech and messages, almost always as a friendly imperative: *Hang tight, I'll be right there.* Coworkers, support agents and doctors' offices use it too, so it's fine in a casual work chat. *Sit tight* means the same and is common in both the US and the UK.
examples: **Hang tight**; I'm just parking the car, and I'll meet you at the entrance in five minutes.
The doctor's running a little behind, so **hang tight** and she'll be with you soon.
I'm checking with my manager about the refund, so **hang tight** for a sec.

drill.sentence: The tow truck is twenty minutes away, so just {{hang tight}} and stay in your car.
drill.hint: wait patiently where you are (US two-word phrase; not *hold on* or the phrase with *sit*)

entries.related: *sit tight* — same meaning, common everywhere; *hang on* / *hold on* — wait a moment, often on the phone; *stay put* — don't move from where you are.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To do something unimportant just to make the time pass while you wait for something.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday speech and fine almost anywhere, including at work. It's often followed by *-ing* or a place (*kill time scrolling on my phone*, *kill time at the mall*), and you can also kill a specific amount: *kill an hour*. Unlike *waste time*, it isn't critical, because there's nothing better to do.
entries.pattern: kill time (+ -ing / at a place); kill an hour
examples: Our flight was delayed three hours, so we **killed time** walking around the airport bookstore.
I got to the restaurant early and **killed half an hour** on my phone at the bar.
When I was a teenager, we used to **kill time** at the mall every Saturday.

drill.sentence: The movie didn't start until nine, so we grabbed a coffee to {{kill time}}.
drill.hint: make the wait go by (two words, with a violent-sounding verb)

entries.related: *pass the time* — same idea, neutral; *waste time* — use time badly, critical; *while away the hours* — spend time in a relaxed way, literary.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To hurry up; to start doing something, or leaving, more quickly.
entries.usage: Casual, mostly an imperative to friends, family or kids (*Get a move on!*), so it can sound impatient or bossy. About yourself it means you need to leave or hurry now: *I'd better get a move on.* Don't say it to customers or your boss; *we need to hurry* is safer.
examples: **Get a move on**, kids, or you're going to miss the bus!
It's already eight, so I'd better **get a move on** if I want to beat the traffic.
If the city doesn't **get a move on** with the bridge repairs, it'll still be closed next winter.

drill.sentence: The ferry leaves in fifteen minutes, so we really need to {{get a move on}}.
drill.hint: start hurrying (four words; not *hurry up* or *pick up the pace*)

entries.related: *hurry up* — the plain version; *step on it* — drive or go faster; *get going* — leave or start, a bit softer.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Busy and active all the time, moving from one task or place to the next with little rest.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, usually after *be* or *keep someone*: *I've been on the go all day*, *Three kids keep me on the go.* It's neutral in tone and fine at work. In ads it often means *while you're traveling or moving* (*snacks for on the go*), a related sense.
examples: I've been **on the go** since six this morning and still haven't had lunch.
My neighbor is eighty-two and still **on the go**: golf on Mondays, volunteering on Wednesdays, poker on Fridays.
Nurses on the night shift are **on the go** for twelve hours straight.

drill.sentence: Between soccer practice, piano lessons and birthday parties, our kids keep us {{on the go}} every weekend.
drill.hint: constantly busy and moving around (three words; not *on our toes*)

entries.related: *busy as a bee* — same idea, a bit old-fashioned; *on your toes* — alert and ready, not busy; *nonstop* — without a break.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: All the time: twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week.
entries.usage: Read it *twenty-four seven*. It works as an adverb (*The gym is open 24/7*) and before a noun (*24/7 customer support*), and in casual talk it often exaggerates (*He's on his phone 24/7*). It's informal, but common in ads and business writing too.
examples: The pharmacy on the corner is open **24/7**, so you can pick up your prescription tonight.
My neighbor's dog barks **twenty-four seven**; I honestly don't know how they sleep.
Being a new parent is a **twenty-four seven** job, and nobody gives you a day off.

drill.sentence: Ever since she got that puppy, my sister texts me pictures of it {{twenty-four seven}}.
drill.hint: all day, every day (said as two numbers; not *nonstop* or *around the clock*)

entries.related: *around the clock* — all day and night, neutral and fine in writing; *nonstop* — without stopping; *all the time* — the plain everyday version.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: I'm leaving now, often quickly or with relief; usually said as *I'm outta here*.
entries.usage: Very casual; said to friends or coworkers when you leave a place, finish work or quit something, often with relief or annoyance. In speech it's nearly always reduced to *I'm outta here*, which is also how people write it in texts. Too casual for a formal goodbye, but fine at the end of a relaxed workday.
examples: Okay, that's my last email for the week. **I'm out of here**; have a good weekend!
If they start arguing about football again, **I'm outta here**.
One more winter of snow and ice, and **I'm out of here**: I'm moving to Arizona.

drill.sentence: My shift's over and I'm exhausted, so {{I'm out of here}}. See you tomorrow!
drill.hint: a casual way to announce you're leaving (four words; not *I'm heading out*)

entries.related: *I'm off* — same, more common in British English; *I'm heading out* — neutral; *I'm gonna take off* — casual American.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Some time ago, usually weeks, months or even years, without saying exactly when.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and emails, usually at the end of the clause: *I saw that movie a while back.* It's vaguer and more relaxed than *some time ago*. *A while ago* means the same, and *quite a while back* suggests a longer time.
examples: I ran into your old roommate **a while back**; he said he's living in Seattle now.
We talked about redoing the kitchen **a while back**, but we never got around to it.
**A while back**, the city promised to fix the potholes on our street, and we're still waiting.

drill.sentence: I lent him my tent {{a while back}}, and he still hasn't returned it.
drill.hint: some time ago (three words; not ending in *ago*)

entries.related: *a while ago* — same meaning; *the other day* — a few days ago; *ages ago* — a long time ago, casual.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go to bed in order to sleep.
entries.usage: Casual and friendly, mostly used to announce that you're going to bed: *I'm gonna hit the sack.* It's about the moment you go to bed and often comes with *early* or *soon* (*I'll hit the sack early tonight*). *Hit the hay* means the same; both are fine with family, roommates and coworkers on a trip.
examples: I'm exhausted, so I'm gonna **hit the sack**; see you guys in the morning.
We have a six a.m. flight, so we should **hit the sack** by ten.
After the camping trip, the kids **hit the sack** without even brushing their teeth.

drill.sentence: It's almost midnight and I have work tomorrow, so I'm going to {{hit the sack}}.
drill.hint: turn in for the night (three words; not ending in *hay*)

entries.related: *hit the hay* — same meaning; *turn in* — go to bed, a bit more neutral; *crash* — fall asleep quickly because you're tired, often somewhere unusual.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Slightly drunk after one or two drinks: relaxed, giggly and a little unsteady, but not seriously drunk.
entries.usage: A light, often humorous word, common in conversation and fine with coworkers at a party: *I'm a little tipsy.* It makes drinking sound harmless, so it's not the word for someone who is very drunk. It often follows *a little*, *a bit* or *slightly*.
examples: After two glasses of wine, Aunt Linda was **tipsy** and telling embarrassing stories about my dad.
I'm a little **tipsy**, so could you drive us home?
We got **tipsy** on margaritas at the beach bar and missed the sunset.

drill.sentence: One beer and she's already {{tipsy}}; she almost never drinks.
drill.hint: slightly drunk (one word; not *buzzed* or *drunk*)

entries.related: *buzzed* — US, the same light effect; *drunk* — the neutral general word; *wasted* — slang, very drunk.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very drunk, or very high on drugs, to the point of losing control.
entries.usage: Slang, common among younger adults in speech and texts, usually with *get* or *be* and often with *totally*, *completely* or *so*. It suggests heavy drinking and lost control, so keep it for friends, not work or older relatives. *Drunk* is the neutral word.
examples: Mark got so **wasted** at the bachelor party that his friends had to put him in a cab.
Don't let your friends drive if they're **wasted**; call them a ride.
In the movie, two college freshmen get **wasted** at their first party and wake up in another city.

drill.sentence: He had six shots in an hour and was completely {{wasted}} by ten o'clock.
drill.hint: extremely drunk (slang, one word; not *hammered*, *trashed* or *smashed*)

entries.related: *tipsy* — only slightly drunk; *hammered* / *trashed* — same meaning, also slang; *high* — affected by drugs, especially marijuana.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Feeling sick, tired and headachy the morning after drinking too much alcohol.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and texts, usually after *be*, *feel* or *wake up*: *I woke up hungover.* The noun is *a hangover* (*I have a terrible hangover*). It's fine to say to friends; at work, admitting you're hungover can sound unprofessional.
examples: I had way too much wine at the wedding and woke up **hungover** with a pounding headache.
He showed up to brunch **hungover**, wearing sunglasses indoors.
Don't plan a seven a.m. hike for New Year's Day; half the group will be **hungover**.

drill.sentence: My roommate was too {{hungover}} to get out of bed until noon.
drill.hint: suffering after last night's drinking (adjective; not *sick*)

mistake.why: *Hangover* is the noun (*have a hangover*); the adjective is *hungover*.

entries.related: *a hangover* — the noun; *the morning after* — the time when you feel the effects; *tipsy* — slightly drunk, long before any hangover.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Extremely good or desirable; so good you would do almost anything to have it.
entries.usage: Casual and enthusiastic, most often about food, but also clothes, views and homes. It usually follows *be* (*The cake was to die for*) or comes right after a noun (*a view to die for*). It's an exaggeration, so it sounds warm and fun in speech and reviews but not in formal writing.
examples: You have to try the tiramisu at that little Italian place; it's **to die for**.
Their apartment is tiny, but it has a rooftop with a view **to die for**.
That leather jacket is **to die for**, but I can't spend four hundred dollars on it.

drill.sentence: My aunt's peach cobbler is {{to die for}}; people fight over the last piece every Thanksgiving.
drill.hint: incredibly good (three words; not *out of this world*)

entries.related: *amazing* — the everyday word; *out of this world* — excellent, also casual; *killer* — slang, very impressive (*a killer view*).

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To get a minor infectious illness, such as a cold or a stomach virus.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and messages when you don't know or don't want to name the illness: *I think I caught a bug.* It's fine in a work message when calling in sick, and you'll often hear *There's a bug going around* (many people are getting sick). *Pick up a bug* means the same.
examples: Half my son's class is home sick, and now he's **caught a bug** too.
I'll have to miss the meeting today; I **caught a bug** over the weekend and can barely get out of bed.
We all **caught a stomach bug** on the cruise and spent two days in our cabin.

drill.sentence: I can't make it to the game tonight; I {{caught a bug}} from my niece, and my stomach's a mess.
drill.hint: got a minor illness (three words; the last one is a word for an insect)

entries.related: *come down with something* — start to get an illness; *a bug going around* — an illness many people have right now; *catch the … bug* — become very enthusiastic (*catch the travel bug*).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Medicine, especially prescription pills that someone takes regularly for a condition.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and among nurses and doctors; it's plural and usually comes with a possessive: *Did you take your meds?* It often refers to long-term medication, including for mental health (*He's doing better since they changed his meds*). In formal writing, use *medication*.
examples: Mom, did you remember to take your blood pressure **meds** this morning?
The night nurse came by at eight to give me my evening **meds**.
Pack your **meds** in your carry-on, not your checked bag, in case your luggage gets lost.

drill.sentence: Our old dog has arthritis, so he'll be on pain {{meds}} for the rest of his life.
drill.hint: short for medication (four letters; not *pills*)

entries.related: *medication* — the neutral, more formal word; *pills* — tablets, informal; *a prescription* — the doctor's order, or the drug itself.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To throw something lightly or casually; very often, to throw something away.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially for throwing away: *Just toss it* means *put it in the trash*. It's lighter and more casual than *throw*, and you also toss things to people (*Toss me the keys*) or onto places (*toss your coat on the bed*). Fine in casual work talk; formal writing uses *discard* or *throw away*.
examples: That milk expired last week; just **toss** it.
Can you **toss** me the remote? It's right next to you.
We **tossed** a bunch of old clothes and books before the move.

drill.sentence: These leftovers have been in the fridge for over a week; we should probably {{toss}} them.
drill.hint: throw away (one casual word; not *dump*, *ditch*, *chuck* or *trash*)

entries.related: *throw out / throw away* — neutral; *ditch* — get rid of, casual; *chuck* — throw or throw away, more common in British English.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To prepare a meal; in the same way, *fix someone a drink* means to make them a drink.
entries.usage: An everyday American use of *fix* meaning *prepare*, common with meals, snacks and drinks: *fix lunch*, *fix yourself a sandwich*, *fix someone a drink*. It sounds casual and homey. *Make dinner* is the neutral choice and the one British speakers use.
entries.pattern: fix + meal; fix someone / yourself + food or drink
examples: I'll **fix dinner** tonight if you can pick up the kids from practice.
When we got home from the airport, my dad **fixed us a drink** and asked about the trip.
There's leftover chicken in the fridge if you want to **fix** yourself a sandwich.

drill.sentence: Mom was in the kitchen {{fixing}} breakfast while we got ready for school.
drill.hint: getting a meal ready (casual US; not *making*, *cooking* or *preparing*)

entries.related: *make dinner* — the neutral version; *cook dinner* — stresses actual cooking; *whip up* — make something quickly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A long trip by car taken for fun, often with friends or family, where the drive itself is part of the experience.
entries.usage: Common in speech and travel writing: *take a road trip*, *go on a road trip*, *a road trip to the Grand Canyon*. It suggests freedom, snacks and music, not a business trip. The idea is strongly linked to American culture, though British speakers now use the phrase too.
examples: After graduation, four of us took **a road trip** down the coast, sleeping in cheap motels.
On our family **road trip** to Yellowstone, the kids fought in the back seat the whole way there.
Download a good playlist before the **road trip**; there's no cell service in the desert.

drill.sentence: We're renting a convertible and taking a {{road trip}} from Chicago to New Orleans this summer.
drill.hint: a long journey by car, just for fun (two words; not *drive*)

entries.related: *a drive* — any car journey, often short; *a getaway* — a short vacation; *a cross-country trip* — a trip across the whole US.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Full of tourists, or made mainly for tourists, often in a way that feels less authentic.
entries.usage: Usually a mild criticism in casual speech and travel reviews: *The old town is a bit touristy.* It often follows *a bit*, *too* or *really*, and it suggests crowds, high prices and souvenir shops. For a neutral description, say *popular with tourists*.
examples: Times Square is way too **touristy** for me; let's get dinner in a quieter neighborhood.
The beach towns down south are more **touristy**, but the beaches up north are almost empty.
I know it's **touristy**, but you can't go to San Francisco and skip the cable cars.

drill.sentence: The restaurant next to the cathedral is overpriced and {{touristy}}; the locals all eat two streets away.
drill.hint: aimed mostly at visitors (one adjective; not *crowded*)

mistake.why: *Touristic* is rare and sounds foreign to Americans; use *touristy*, or *tourist* before a noun (*a tourist area*).

entries.related: *a tourist trap* — a place that overcharges tourists; *off the beaten path* — away from tourist areas; *popular with tourists* — the neutral phrase.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A shop, restaurant or attraction that charges too much and exists mainly to get money from tourists.
entries.usage: Clearly critical, used in conversation, travel reviews and articles: *That restaurant is a total tourist trap.* It's stronger than *touristy*, which only means full of tourists or made for them. Common with *total*, *classic* or *a bit of a*.
examples: Don't eat on the main square; those places are **tourist traps** with frozen food and twenty-dollar salads.
The "historic" gold mine turned out to be **a tourist trap** with a huge gift shop and a five-minute tour.
Some people call Niagara Falls **a tourist trap**, but the falls themselves are amazing.

drill.sentence: We paid fifteen dollars for a bottle of water at that place; it's a total {{tourist trap}}.
drill.hint: an overpriced spot that targets visitors (two words; not *rip-off*)

entries.related: *touristy* — full of or made for tourists, milder; *a rip-off* — anything overpriced; *a hidden gem* — a great place few tourists know.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To search for something on the internet, whatever search engine you use.
entries.usage: Extremely common in speech and casual writing, as a regular verb: *google, googled, googling*. People also google a person to find information about them (*I googled him before the interview*). Dictionaries list it lowercase, though you'll also see *Google*; in formal writing, *search for* or *look up online* is safer.
examples: I didn't know what the word meant, so I **googled** it.
Before their first date, she **googled** him and found an old blog about his band.
Stop **googling** your symptoms; you'll just convince yourself it's something serious.

drill.sentence: I can't remember who sings this song. Hang on, let me {{google}} it.
drill.hint: search for it online (a company's name used as a verb)

entries.related: *look something up* — find information, online or in a book; *search for* — more neutral; *do a quick search* — work-friendly phrasing.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A small, usually temporary technical problem that stops something from working properly.
entries.usage: Common in speech, news and work emails, and neutral enough for most writing: *a glitch in the system*, *a technical glitch*. It suggests a minor, short problem, so companies like the word when they want a failure to sound small. It's also used loosely for small problems in plans (*one small glitch*).
examples: A **glitch** in the airline's booking system canceled hundreds of reservations overnight.
Sorry I didn't reply; some **glitch** on my phone deleted all my texts.
The wedding went perfectly except for one small **glitch**: the cake arrived an hour late.

drill.sentence: The TV froze during the last five minutes of the game because of a {{glitch}} in the streaming app.
drill.hint: something briefly going wrong with the technology (one word; not *bug*, *error*, *issue* or *problem*)

entries.related: *a bug* — an error in software code; *a hiccup* — a small delay or problem in a plan; *a snag* — an unexpected problem.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Old, worthless or unwanted things, especially things that take up space.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech: *The garage is full of junk.* It's uncountable (*a lot of junk*, not *junks*). It also appears in many everyday compounds: *junk food*, *junk mail*, and *a junk drawer* (a kitchen drawer for random small items).
examples: We spent the whole weekend hauling **junk** out of the garage before the new owners moved in.
Why do you keep all this **junk**? You haven't used that bread maker in ten years.
The yard sale was mostly **junk**, but I found a great lamp for five bucks.

drill.sentence: Before we move, we need to get rid of all the {{junk}} in the attic: broken chairs, old magazines and boxes of cables.
drill.hint: worthless old things (one word; not *stuff*, *clutter* or *trash*)

entries.related: *stuff* — things in general, not negative; *clutter* — too many things in a messy space; *trash* — US, waste you throw away.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be stopped by the police while driving, usually for breaking a traffic law.
entries.usage: The normal everyday phrase in American English, common in speech and news: *I got pulled over for speeding.* It's a *get* passive; the active form is *The officer pulled me over*. Usually with *for* + the reason (*for speeding*, *for a broken taillight*).
examples: I **got pulled over** for going fifty in a thirty, and the ticket cost me two hundred dollars.
My daughter **got pulled over** last night for rolling through a stop sign.
If you **get pulled over**, keep your hands on the wheel and wait for the officer.

drill.sentence: He'd been driving with expired tags for months, so it was only a matter of time before he {{got pulled over}}.
drill.hint: was stopped by the police (three words; not *got stopped*)

entries.related: *pull over* — stop at the side of the road; *get a ticket* — receive a fine; *get stopped* — same meaning, less specific.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who is new to a job, activity, place or online community and is still learning how things work.
entries.usage: Casual and usually friendly, often used about yourself: *I'm a total newbie at golf.* Said by others, it can sound a little condescending, especially online, where *noob* is the mocking gaming version. At work, *new hire* is the neutral term.
examples: I'm a total **newbie** at skiing, so please don't take me down the steep runs.
The **newbies** in our running club always start too fast and burn out by mile three.
As the only **newbie** on the team, I spent my first week just learning who did what.

drill.sentence: Be patient with him; he's a {{newbie}} and doesn't know where anything is in the kitchen yet.
drill.hint: someone new to this (one word; not *rookie*, *beginner* or *newcomer*)

entries.related: *a rookie* — US, a first-year player or worker; *a beginner* — neutral; *a newcomer* — someone who has just arrived.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is very skilled at something, often surprisingly quick or talented.
entries.usage: Casual and admiring, usually with a noun in front or with *at* or *with*: *a math whiz*, *a computer whiz*, *a whiz at crosswords*, *a whiz with numbers*. Common in American speech and journalism (*a twelve-year-old chess whiz*). British English spells it *whizz* or says *wizard*.
entries.pattern: a + noun + whiz; a whiz at / with something
examples: My niece is a math **whiz**; she was doing algebra in fourth grade.
Ask Carlos to fix the dishwasher; he's a **whiz** with anything mechanical.
My roommate is a **whiz** at crossword puzzles and does the Sunday one in pen.

drill.sentence: Let Jenny do the taxes this year; she's a real {{whiz}} with numbers.
drill.hint: a very skilled person (one word; not *wizard*, *genius* or *pro*)

entries.related: *a whiz kid* — a young person who is very talented; *a pro* — someone skilled, often professional; *a natural* — someone talented from the start.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is very interested in studying, technology or a specialized hobby, and is sometimes seen as socially awkward.
entries.usage: Once mainly an insult, it's now often neutral or affectionate, and many people proudly call themselves nerds. *A* + topic + *nerd* shows passion (*a history nerd*, *a coffee nerd*), and *nerd out about* something means talk about your hobby with great excitement. Said in a mocking tone, especially among kids, it still hurts.
examples: I was a total **nerd** in high school: chess club, math team and straight A's.
Don't get my brother started on coffee beans; he's a real coffee **nerd**.
Some kids called him a **nerd** for reading at recess, but he didn't care.

drill.sentence: My dad reads every manual cover to cover and tracks his car's gas mileage in a notebook; he's such a {{nerd}}.
drill.hint: a person obsessed with details and facts (one word; not *geek* or *dork*)

entries.related: *a geek* — similar, often about technology or fan culture; *a dork* — awkward and silly, not necessarily smart; *a bookworm* — someone who loves reading.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who reacts to small problems as if they were disasters, with too much emotion and attention-seeking.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, but often teasing between friends and family: *Stop being such a drama queen.* It's used about men too, even though *queen* is in the phrase. It sounds dismissive if someone is really upset, so avoid it when the problem is serious.
examples: He got a paper cut and acted like he needed an ambulance; what a **drama queen**.
My cat is such a **drama queen**: she screams if her food bowl is half empty.
Don't be a **drama queen**; it's one bad review, not the end of your career.

drill.sentence: My sister burned the toast and announced that her whole day was ruined; she's such a {{drama queen}}.
drill.hint: someone who overreacts emotionally (two words; not *crybaby*)

entries.related: *overreact* — the neutral verb; *a crybaby* — someone who cries or complains too easily, childish; *make a scene* — behave emotionally in public.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who spends a lot of time sitting and watching TV and gets very little exercise.
entries.usage: Casual and humorous, often said about yourself or with gentle criticism: *I turned into a couch potato over the holidays.* It's a mild tease, not a serious insult. Common with *become*, *turn into* or *total*.
examples: Since he retired, my dad has become a total **couch potato**; he watches golf all day.
After two weeks of rain, the whole family turned into **couch potatoes**.
Our dog is a **couch potato**; he'd rather nap than go for a walk.

drill.sentence: I promised myself I'd start running this winter instead of being a {{couch potato}} every weekend.
drill.hint: someone who lies around watching TV (two words; not *lazy bum*)

entries.related: *a homebody* — someone who likes being at home, not necessarily lazy; *a slob* — messy and lazy; *a gym rat* — someone who spends a lot of time at the gym.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who enjoys being with other people and is good at talking to them and getting along with them.
entries.usage: Positive and casual, common in conversation, job interviews and job ads: *I'm a people person.* In interviews it's so common that it can sound like a cliché, so back it up with an example. *Not a people person* is a soft, humorous way to say you prefer being alone.
examples: Sarah's a real **people person**; she knows the names of everyone in our building.
I'm not really a **people person** before my first cup of coffee.
We need a **people person** at the front desk, someone who stays friendly when guests get angry.

drill.sentence: Our mail carrier knows every dog on the street by name and stops to chat with everyone; she's a real {{people person}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves being around others (two words; not *social butterfly*)

entries.related: *a social butterfly* — someone who moves happily between many people at events; *outgoing* — friendly and sociable; *an introvert* — someone who gets energy from being alone.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An energetic, ambitious person who works hard and takes action to get what they want.
entries.usage: Positive and upbeat, common in talk about work and careers, and in job ads and reference letters. It suggests initiative: a go-getter doesn't wait to be told what to do. *Self-starter* is the more formal job-ad word.
examples: Emma's a real **go-getter**; she started her own dog-walking business at fifteen.
We're looking for a **go-getter** who can bring in new clients without much supervision.
My mom was a **go-getter** who went from cleaning offices to running her own cleaning company.

drill.sentence: She's a real {{go-getter}}: two jobs, night classes, and she still finds time to train for marathons.
drill.hint: an ambitious, energetic person (hyphenated noun; not *high achiever*)

entries.related: *a self-starter* — someone who works without being told, job-ad language; *ambitious* — the neutral adjective; *an overachiever* — someone who does more than expected, sometimes too much.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is very interested in good food, enjoys trying new dishes and restaurants, and often likes to cook.
entries.usage: Casual and usually positive, often used about yourself: *I'm a bit of a foodie.* It's about interest in quality and new trends, not about eating a lot. Some people find the word a little pretentious, so it's also used with gentle irony (*foodie places with tiny portions*).
examples: My brother's a huge **foodie**; he plans his vacations around the restaurants he wants to try.
This neighborhood used to be quiet, but now it's full of **foodie** spots with long lines.
As a **foodie**, she was horrified when her boyfriend put ketchup on her homemade pasta.

drill.sentence: Ask Dana where to eat in Chicago; she's a real {{foodie}} and knows all the best places.
drill.hint: someone passionate about good food (one word; not *gourmet* or *food lover*)

entries.related: *a gourmet* — a more formal word for a food expert; *a food snob* — a foodie who looks down on ordinary food; *a picky eater* — someone who eats only a few foods.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who works too much and finds it hard to stop working or relax.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and journalism, often as a mild criticism or a worried comment, though some people say it about themselves almost proudly. It's made from *work* + *-aholic* (as in *alcoholic*), a pattern also used jokingly in *chocoholic* and *shopaholic*.
examples: My dad was a **workaholic** who answered emails at the dinner table every night.
She calls herself a recovering **workaholic**; she now turns her phone off on weekends.
I'm not a **workaholic**; I just have a demanding boss and too many deadlines.

drill.sentence: He took his laptop on our honeymoon and answered work calls on the beach; he's a total {{workaholic}}.
drill.hint: someone addicted to their job (one word; not *overachiever*)

entries.related: *type A* — competitive, driven and impatient; *burned out* — exhausted from too much work; *a slacker* — the opposite, someone who avoids work.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is very interested in a subject and knows a lot about it, as a hobby rather than a job.
entries.usage: Almost always after a noun naming the subject: *a history buff*, *a movie buff*, *a Civil War buff*, *a wine buff*. It's casual and positive, used in conversation and journalism. Don't confuse it with the adjective *buff*, which means muscular (*He got really buff*).
examples: My father-in-law is a huge history **buff** and can name every battle of the Civil War.
Any wine **buff** will tell you that expensive doesn't always mean better.
The train museum is run by volunteers, mostly retired railroad **buffs**.

drill.sentence: Ask Ted about any old Western; he's a real movie {{buff}} and has seen them all.
drill.hint: an enthusiast who knows a lot (one short word; not *fan*, *nerd* or *geek*)

entries.related: *an enthusiast* — more formal; *a fan* — someone who loves something, not necessarily an expert; *a nerd* — very interested, sometimes socially awkward.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An insult for someone seen as unsuccessful, pathetic or uncool.
entries.usage: A common, fairly harsh insult among kids and teens and in casual adult talk; between close friends it can be playful. Calling yourself one is a typical self-mocking joke (*I'm such a loser; I stayed home all weekend*). In neutral use it just means the one who loses, as in *a good loser* or *a sore loser*.
examples: My friends think he's a **loser** because he's thirty-five and still borrowing money from his mom.
In high school, the popular kids called anyone in the chess club a **loser**.
I'm such a **loser**; I forgot my own sister's birthday again.

drill.sentence: Don't let anyone call you a {{loser}} just because you didn't make the team this year.
drill.hint: a cruel word for someone unsuccessful (not *failure*)

entries.related: *a sore loser* — someone who complains when they lose; *a failure* — someone who failed, more serious; *a nobody* — an unimportant person.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An important, powerful or influential person, especially in business or a local community.
entries.usage: Casual and often a little mocking or envious: *Look at you, Mr. Big Shot.* It can be neutral (*some big shot from headquarters*), but it often suggests that the person thinks they're very important. Before a noun it's hyphenated: *a big-shot lawyer*.
examples: Some **big shot** from headquarters is visiting, so everyone's cleaning their desks.
Now that he's a **big shot** at a law firm, he never has time for his old friends.
The mayor and a few local **big shots** cut the ribbon at the new hospital.

drill.sentence: My little brother got his driver's license and now struts around like a {{big shot}}.
drill.hint: a very important person (two words; not *hotshot* or *VIP*)

entries.related: *a hotshot* — a confident, successful person, often young; *a bigwig* — similar, slightly old-fashioned; *a VIP* — a very important person, neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is good at something from the very start, without much training or effort.
entries.usage: Warm praise, common in speech: *You're a natural!* Often followed by *at* + activity (*a natural at public speaking*) or *on* for stage, camera or a playing field (*a natural on camera*). It's informal but fine at work, for example after someone's first presentation.
entries.pattern: a natural (at + activity / on camera, on stage)
examples: It was her first time on a surfboard, and she stood up right away; the instructor said she was **a natural**.
My son's **a natural** on the piano; he plays songs by ear after hearing them once.
Great job leading the meeting; you're **a natural** at this.

drill.sentence: He'd never held a golf club before, but he hit the ball perfectly on his first swing; he's {{a natural}}.
drill.hint: someone with an inborn talent (two words; not *a pro*)

entries.related: *gifted* / *talented* — the neutral adjectives; *a pro* — someone with experience and skill; *have a knack for* — be naturally good at something specific.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A rude, badly behaved child, especially one who is spoiled and used to getting everything.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, usually said about other people's children, or with affection about your own family (*my bratty little brother*). It very often comes with *spoiled*: *a spoiled brat*. Said about an adult who acts like a spoiled child, it's a real insult.
examples: The kid behind us on the plane kicked my seat for three hours; what a **brat**.
She was a total **brat** as a kid, but she grew up to be really sweet.
Stop acting like a spoiled **brat** and apologize to your cousin.

drill.sentence: The boy screamed in the toy store until his dad bought him a third toy; he's such a spoiled {{brat}}.
drill.hint: badly behaved child (one word; not *kid* or *child*)

entries.related: *bratty* — the adjective; *spoiled* — given too much, so badly behaved; *a military brat* — US, a child of a military family, not an insult.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who is weak, timid or easily scared, and avoids anything difficult, painful or risky.
entries.usage: Casual and mildly insulting, often teasing between friends or used about yourself: *I'm such a wimp about horror movies.* Common with *about* + thing (*a wimp about the cold*). The phrasal verb *wimp out* means not do something because you're scared.
examples: Come on, don't be a **wimp**; the water's not that cold once you get in.
I'm a total **wimp** about needles; I have to look away when they take blood.
My husband's a **wimp** when he has a cold; he acts like he's dying.

drill.sentence: My brother refused to go on the roller coaster because it looked too scary; he's such a {{wimp}}.
drill.hint: a scared, weak person (one word; not *chicken*, *baby* or *coward*)

entries.related: *a chicken* — someone too scared to do something; *a coward* — stronger and more serious; *wimp out (of something)* — not do something because you're afraid.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Always telling other people what to do, in an annoying or controlling way.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, very common about children, siblings, coworkers and partners: *Stop being so bossy.* It describes a manner, not real authority: a manager isn't bossy just for giving instructions, only for giving them in a pushy way. In formal feedback, *domineering* or *controlling* fit better.
examples: My older sister was so **bossy** when we were kids; she even told me how to hold my crayons.
Our new neighbor is a little **bossy**; she's already told us where to put our trash cans.
I don't mean to sound **bossy**, but can everyone please put their dishes in the dishwasher?

drill.sentence: Nobody wants to be in Kyle's group because he's so {{bossy}} and never listens to anyone.
drill.hint: always giving orders (one word; not *controlling* or *pushy*)

entries.related: *pushy* — pressuring people to do things; *controlling* — trying to control others, more serious; *domineering* — formal, very bossy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Too emotionally dependent on someone, always wanting to be with them and needing their attention.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, common about partners in dating talk (*He's getting kind of clingy*), often together with *needy*. About toddlers and pets it's softer and often describes normal behavior (*a clingy toddler*, *a clingy cat*).
examples: She texts him every ten minutes when he's out with friends; she's a little **clingy**.
Our toddler gets really **clingy** when he's tired and won't let me put him down.
The dog has been so **clingy** since we got back from vacation; she follows me from room to room.

drill.sentence: I like him, but he gets upset whenever I see my friends without him; he's a little too {{clingy}}.
drill.hint: too dependent on me (one word; not *needy*, *jealous* or *possessive*)

entries.related: *needy* — always needing attention or reassurance; *possessive* — wanting to control a partner; *attached* — emotionally close, neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Unfriendly to others because you think you are better or more important than they are.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, very common among teens and in everyday talk about people who seem cold or snobbish: *She's kind of stuck-up.* It's usually written with a hyphen. More formal words are *arrogant* and *snobbish*.
examples: I thought the new girl was **stuck-up**, but it turns out she's just really shy.
The people at that country club are so **stuck-up**; nobody even said hello to us.
He got a little **stuck-up** after his band got famous.

drill.sentence: She walks past everyone in the office without saying hi, so people think she's {{stuck-up}}.
drill.hint: thinks she's better than others (hyphenated; not *snobby*, *snooty* or *arrogant*)

entries.related: *snobby* — looking down on people of lower status or taste; *full of yourself* — too proud of yourself; *down-to-earth* — the opposite, friendly and unpretentious.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Friendly and nice to someone's face but saying unkind things about them behind their back.
entries.usage: Casual and strongly critical: calling someone *two-faced* accuses them of dishonesty and disloyalty, common in talk about friends, coworkers and family. Usually after *be* (*She's so two-faced*) or before *person* or *friend*. Younger speakers often say *fake* for the same idea.
examples: She's sweet to me in meetings, then complains about me to the boss; she's so **two-faced**.
I can't stand **two-faced** people who smile at you and then gossip the minute you leave.
My neighbor praised our new fence, then called the city to complain about it; how **two-faced** is that?

drill.sentence: He was all smiles at the party, but later I heard him making fun of my cooking. I didn't know he was so {{two-faced}}.
drill.hint: nice to you in person but unkind behind your back (hyphenated; not *fake*)

entries.related: *fake* — insincere, slang among younger people; *backstabbing* — betraying people who trust you; *hypocritical* — saying one thing and doing another.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Talking nonsense, exaggerating or lying, especially in a confident way.
entries.usage: Casual and fairly blunt, said when you don't believe someone: *Oh, you're so full of it!* Between friends it's often playful, but to a stranger or a boss it's rude. It's a milder form of a vulgar expression, so keep it out of work conversations.
examples: He says he ran a marathon in under three hours? He's **full of it**.
Oh, you're so **full of it**; you've never even been to Paris.
That car salesman was **full of it**: the "one-owner" car had been in three accidents.

drill.sentence: My brother swears he once beat a pro tennis player, but I think he's {{full of it}}.
drill.hint: talking nonsense (three words; not the phrase ending in *baloney*)

entries.related: *full of baloney* — same, softer and old-fashioned; *making it up* — inventing a story; *pulling someone's leg* — telling a false story as a joke.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To treat someone unkindly again and again, for example by teasing, criticizing or bullying them, often because they are weaker.
entries.usage: Common in speech about kids, siblings and coworkers, often with *stop* or *always*: *Stop picking on your sister!* It can also mean single someone out unfairly for criticism (*Why are you picking on me?*). *Pick on someone your own size* is a common rebuke to a bully.
examples: The older kids on the bus used to **pick on** him because of his glasses.
My manager keeps **picking on** me in meetings, criticizing every small thing I say.
Quit **picking on** your little brother; he's only five.

drill.sentence: My big sister {{picked on}} me constantly when we were kids, but now she's my best friend.
drill.hint: treated unkindly again and again (two words; not *teased*, *bullied* or *messed with*)

entries.related: *bully* — hurt or threaten someone weaker, more serious; *tease* — make fun of someone, often playfully; *single someone out* — choose one person for special treatment, often unfair.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To behave in a silly or playful way instead of doing something serious, or to spend time doing nothing useful.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, especially to kids and teens: *Stop messing around and finish your homework.* *Mess around with* + thing means play with it or change it carelessly (*Don't mess around with the settings*). Careful: *mess around with* + person can mean have a casual sexual or romantic relationship.
examples: The boys were **messing around** in class and got sent to the principal's office.
We didn't do much on Sunday, just **messed around** at the beach and ate ice cream.
Someone's been **messing around** with the thermostat; it's eighty degrees in here.

drill.sentence: Stop {{messing around}} and get dressed; the bus will be here in five minutes!
drill.hint: acting silly instead of getting ready (two words; not *fooling …*, *goofing …* or *horsing …*)

entries.related: *fool around* — same, but it also has a sexual meaning; *goof off* — US, waste time instead of working; *mess about* — the British version.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A sudden moment when someone completely loses emotional control, for example by crying, shouting or panicking.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk about toddlers (*a meltdown in the supermarket*) and, with humor, about adults under stress. Use *have a meltdown*, often with *total* or *complete*. The word also means a collapse of a system or market (*a financial meltdown*), from the meltdown of a nuclear reactor.
examples: My two-year-old had a total **meltdown** in the cereal aisle because I said no to cookies.
I almost had a **meltdown** when I realized my passport had expired two days before our flight.
My boss had a **meltdown** when the printer jammed five minutes before the client meeting.

drill.sentence: When the airline canceled our flight for the third time, my normally calm mother had a complete {{meltdown}} at the gate.
drill.hint: a total loss of emotional control (one word; not *breakdown*, *tantrum* or *freakout*)

entries.related: *a tantrum* — a child's angry outburst; *a breakdown* — a serious mental-health crisis; *lose it* — informal, suddenly become very upset or angry.
